questions.evidence:
During a school waste-sorting activity, two classes inspect their recycling bins before collection. Class A finds twenty correctly sorted items out of twenty-five. Class B finds twenty-four correctly sorted items out of forty. The classes use the same sorting checklist and count each item once.

A student says Class B did better because twenty-four is larger than twenty. Another asks to consider how many items were checked in each class. Having more correct items does not necessarily mean a larger share of the bin was sorted correctly.

Class A's share is eighty percent, while Class B's is sixty percent. The report includes both counts and percentages. It describes only the bins examined on that day, since neither group has kept a long-term record of its usual sorting habits.

Both classes choose one common mistake from their own bin and make a clearer label for the following week. The goal is to improve decisions at the bin, not turn one small check into a permanent label about which class is more responsible.
options: Both have 80% correct because their counts exceed twenty.
B has 100% correct because twenty-four is larger.
A has 80% correct and B has 60% correct.
A has 60% correct and B has 80% correct.
